Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' is inconsistent as written: it is phrased like a trigger ('seeing people...') rather than a strategy the patient uses. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, the other items are clear coping behaviours, so this item is internally mismatched.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as clinically poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The other strategies are avoidance/disengagement (screen use, avoiding people), and the threat/memory profile is hypervigilance plus overwhelm. This item introduces a much more extreme coping style without supporting indicators elsewhere in the five target components, making the strategy set feel internally uneven for the same patient.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma in a 46-year-old civilian graphic designer, self-blame for 'the way I acted' is possible, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals that frame the trauma as globally ruining life and draining meaning, without any other items suggesting perceived responsibility, moral failure, or a specific behavior during the event. The appraisal set is therefore less coherent than the other nodes.

vignette: The call went out for a welfare check that escalated into a foot pursuit through the narrow alleys of the old industrial district. Elias Vance was forty-two then, still carrying the weight of his badge. He remembered the exact pressure of his own hands holding the suspect’s shoulders, the sharp crack of bone against concrete, and the way the man’s mouth split open, leaving a raw, bleeding wound that did not stop flowing. The silence that followed the ambulance was heavier than the sirens. Months later, the internal review dismissed the restraint as procedurally standard, offering no acknowledgment of the split-second gravity he had carried. That specific history is what makes the present-day landscape so unforgiving. In the weeks that followed, his body refused to return to rest. He would stand in his kitchen doorway, eyes automatically tracking the far exits before he could reach for his coffee. His shoulders stayed elevated, his forearms coiled, his breathing shallow. When his wife tried to speak with him about the coming months, the words caught in his throat. He would begin to describe the night of the chase, but the memory did not arrive as a narrative. It arrived as a sudden, suffocating pressure in his chest, accompanied by the vivid sight of a fractured lip or a bruised temple that was not in the room. The emotional weight was so immediate that he had to stop mid-sentence, breathless, because he could not carry it. He has come to believe that the man he was before that night is gone, and the department’s silence only deepened his conviction that what happened to him was deeply unfair, that nothing has been done about it. Now at forty-six, working as a freelance graphic designer, Elias navigates a daily environment that constantly mirrors the past. He keeps his studio blinds drawn, but when he opens them to review a client’s editorial layout featuring a staged car accident, the sight of a model’s bandaged leg sends a jolt straight down his spine. His mind floods with the exact angle of the suspect’s jaw against the pavement. He pulls the blinds shut, heart hammering against his ribs. The presence of authority is worse. Even a parked police cruiser idling outside his building’s driveway triggers an immediate, unyielding need to leave. He stops taking client meetings at their offices. He scans every room—the coffee shop, the design gallery, the therapy waiting area—mapping the nearest door, the placement of furniture that could shield him. He cannot relax knowing his phone is on the desk. Instead, he loses hours to digital spaces, scrolling through games and forums, forcing his mind to run on a different track so the old footage does not catch up. He avoids people now. Conversations feel like walking on thin ice. His wife notices the distance, the way he flinches when a door slams or when she reaches for his shoulder. Nothing in his current work feels significant compared to the void left behind. He is certain that his life was irreparably broken that day in the alleys. It is this accumulating exhaustion that finally brings him to counseling. He sits in the therapist’s office, hands flat on his knees, scanning the windows and the door behind the chair. He wants to explain why he cannot stay in a room without calculating his exit, why the sight of a bruise on a stranger’s knuckle stops his breath, why his own thoughts feel like constant betrayals. He hopes, more than anything, to find a way to sit in a room without bracing for danger, and to sleep without his body waiting for a fight that is no longer there.
